content: The transmission of dengue viruses occurs primarily through mosquito vectors, with a lesser extent of cases linked to mosquitoes transported via aircraft. Although the risk of such transmission is minimal, the World Health Organization (WHO) has deemed it necessary to address this issue. In 2018, a WHO consultation identified the need for standardized guidance on aircraft disinsection methods and procedures, including the development of standard operating procedures. This does not preclude the testing and evaluation of alternative methods for potential approval or recommendation by WHO. The first edition of the WHO guidelines on aircraft disinsection methods and procedures was published in 2021 to address these requirements. The current document provides an update to the first edition, focusing on effective disinsection methods and procedures. However, it does not comprehensively address all aspects of aircraft disinsection, such as regulatory approval of products or occupational risk assessments. The document is specifically concerned with controlling arthropods, primarily insect vectors of disease, within the cabin, flight deck, and cargo areas of aircraft. Separate guidance exists for vector surveillance and control in and around airport premises. While the prevention of agricultural pest importation is outside the scope of this document, many countries mandate aircraft disinsection for this purpose. The guidance is intended for use by various stakeholders, including the airline industry, airport authorities, national pesticide regulatory agencies, the pesticide industry, public health and pest control organizations, aviation authorities, and other relevant parties. Aircraft disinsection products must comply with national pesticide registration requirements, the specifications outlined in this document, national aviation policies, aircraft manufacturers’ technical and safety standards, and practices recommended by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Only disinsection products that have been thoroughly tested by aircraft manufacturers or laboratories to ensure they do not damage aircraft materials (e.g., plexiglass, plastics, metals) are approved for use. Manufacturers must provide pesticide product labels and safety data sheets to airlines or disinsection applicators for each product used. WHO has published guidance on testing the efficacy of aircraft disinsection products and a generic risk assessment model with examples and evaluations of different product types. A systematic review on the safety and applicability of pyrethroid insecticides for aircraft disinsection was conducted in 2020. Currently, pyrethroids such as permethrin and d-phenothrin (or 1R-trans-phenothrin) are the primary insecticides recommended for aircraft disinsection. Permethrin provides residual effects on surfaces, while d-phenothrin primarily offers knockdown and killing effects with limited residual efficacy. No alternative pesticides have been prequalified to replace pyrethroids in cases of mosquito resistance. Pesticides are applied in passenger cabins, including toilet areas and cargo holds, using aerosols and residual surface treatments. The flight deck, cockpit, and crew rest areas are treated with aerosol applications only. Aerosol dispensers are used to treat all accessible spaces, and overhead luggage rack doors should remain open until spraying is complete. WHO specifications for aerosol dispensers require that the entire contents be discharged as an aerosol within a specified time without interruption. For space treatments, droplets smaller than 30 μm in diameter are required to remain airborne for extended periods, with optimal droplet sizes between 10–15 μm for effective mosquito control. Aerosol products must meet specific physical requirements, such as limiting droplets larger than 30 μm to ≤20% by weight and droplets larger than 50 μm to ≤1% by weight. These requirements may not be met during the discharge of the last 10% of the aerosol can’s contents. Aerosol application aims to quickly knock down and kill small flying insects present in the cabin airspace. Permethrin, which acts more slowly, is used to treat cabin spaces and provide a fine residual coating on internal surfaces. When insects contact treated surfaces, they are knocked down to the floor. Aerosol cans should have a discharge rate of 1 g/s (±20%) and produce droplet sizes according to WHO specifications. The recommended spray rates for cabin and cargo holds are as follows: Cabin spraying: 10 g of formulation per 28 m³ (1,000 ft³). Cargo hold spraying: Increased from 10 g/28 m³ to 40 g/28 m³ for lower cargo holds and 15 g/28 m³ for upper cargo hold areas of freighters. Residual application is an alternative method for empty aircraft, providing a persistent insecticidal deposit effective for up to 8 weeks. This method involves treating all internal surfaces, including cargo areas and passenger cabins, with permethrin 2% emulsifiable concentrate (EC). The flight deck, cockpit, and crew rest areas are treated with permethrin 2% aerosol instead of residual treatment. Equipment for residual treatment must comply with WHO specifications for vector control equipment. The equipment should produce spray droplets with a volume median diameter (Dv) of ≥50 μm, with no more than 10% of droplets smaller than 30 μm to minimize inhalation risks. Operators must be trained to configure equipment correctly, apply the appropriate technique for even distribution, and maintain the correct swath width. Electrostatic sprayers, which generate charged spray droplets for better coverage, have been used extensively for aircraft disinfection but not for disinsection. These sprayers must produce charged droplets with specific size parameters and be designed to direct the spray to target surfaces effectively. The use of personal protective equipment (PPE) is essential during disinsection and pesticide handling to reduce operator exposure. PPE selection should follow the insecticide manufacturer’s product label and adhere to FAO/WHO guidance on pesticide risk reduction. Pesticide products, including spray cans, must meet regulatory requirements, such as manufacturer specifications approved by national pesticide registration authorities or WHO specifications, compliance with international standards, and adherence to regulations in both departure and arrival countries. Airlines may require additional testing to meet aircraft manufacturer specifications. Testing of alternative chemicals for aircraft application must evaluate efficacy, human safety, and material safety.
